subject: Physiology
summary: Intestinal absorption is the process by which nutrients and electrolytes cross the gut epithelium into circulation. It relies on active transport, facilitated diffusion, and paracellular pathways, all regulated by hormones and local factors. Clinicians must assess absorption defects to diagnose malnutrition, infections, and metabolic disorders.

sections.p: The small intestine is the main site for absorption of macronutrients, micronutrients, and water. The mucosal surface is maximised by villi and microvilli, and transporters on enterocytes mediate selective uptake.
b: Enterocytes are the main absorptive cells

sections.p: Nutrients enter cells via active transport (e.g., sodium‑glucose cotransport), facilitated diffusion (e.g., glucose via GLUT2), or passive paracellular flow. Water follows osmotic gradients.
b: Paracellular pores allow ions and water

t.b: Assess for hypokalemia or hyponatremia indicating malabsorption or diarrhea; high levels suggest renal loss or over‑replacement
Detect steatorrhea; high fat indicates pancreatic insufficiency or bile acid deficiency
Evaluate proximal small bowel function; low absorption suggests villous atrophy or celiac disease

sections.p: Hormones such as PTH and vitamin D enhance calcium absorption; gastrin and secretin influence fluid secretion; local cytokines modulate transporter expression.
b: PTH ↑ 1α‑hydroxylase → more active vitamin D → ↑ calcium uptake

t.b: Low levels predict impaired calcium absorption; high levels may indicate hypervitaminosis

sections.p: Common causes of impaired absorption include celiac disease, tropical sprue, Crohn’s disease, bacterial overgrowth, pancreatic insufficiency, and drug effects.
b: Bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine

t.b: Positive in celiac disease; confirms diagnosis
Low indicates pancreatic insufficiency; guides enzyme replacement

sections.p: Malabsorption leads to weight loss, anemia, electrolyte disturbances, and growth failure. Recognising patterns guides targeted investigations and therapy.

t.b: Anemia type (iron, B12, folate) directs nutrient deficiency
Low indicates protein loss or malnutrition

sections.p: Remember that calcium absorption is vitamin D‑dependent; PTH indirectly increases it. In tropical settings, consider schistosomiasis and malaria affecting gut integrity.

t.b: Low in vitamin D deficiency; high in hyperparathyroidism

sections.p: Treat underlying cause (e.g., gluten‑free diet for celiac, enzyme replacement for pancreatitis). Provide nutritional support and monitor electrolytes.

t.b: Correct deficiency; monitor serum calcium and phosphate

sections.p: Intestinal obstruction mimics malabsorption but presents with abdominal pain and vomiting. Diarrhea can be due to infection rather than absorption defect.
Serum electrolytes may be normal early; fecal fat can be falsely low if diet is low in fat. Stool elastase may be normal in mild pancreatic insufficiency.

faq.q: What is the difference between active and passive absorption?
faq.a: Active transport uses energy and carriers; passive relies on concentration gradients.

faq.q: Why does vitamin D matter for calcium absorption?
faq.a: It upregulates calcium transporters in enterocytes, increasing intestinal uptake.
Yes, bacterial overgrowth, parasites, and viral enteritis can damage villi and impair uptake.
